title: Git & Linux
subtitle: The commands you reach for every day

cards.prompt: How do you turn the current folder into a new Git repository?
cards.note: This creates the hidden `.git` folder that holds the entire history. Delete it and the project is just an ordinary folder again.

cards.prompt: How do you download an existing repository, for example from GitHub, for the first time?
cards.note: `git clone <url>` fetches the entire history, not just the latest state. Afterwards `origin` is set up as the remote automatically.

cards.prompt: Which command shows which files are changed or staged?
cards.note: It is the command you should type most often, before every commit. `git status -s` shows the same in a compact form.

cards.prompt: How do you stage changes for the next commit?
cards.note: `git add -p` walks through the changes hunk by hunk so you can pick exactly what goes in. That keeps commits small and clean.

cards.prompt: How do you commit with a message right on the command line?
cards.note: Keep the first line short and in the imperative, such as "Fix login timeout". Without `-m`, Git opens your editor for longer messages.

cards.prompt: How do you show the commit history in compact form?
cards.note: Add `--graph --all` to also see how branches split off and join again.

cards.prompt: How do you see line by line what you have changed since the last commit?
cards.note: `git diff` shows unstaged changes, while `git diff --staged` shows what will go into the next commit.

cards.prompt: How do you create a new branch and switch to it right away?
cards.note: `git switch -c feature` is the modern form of `git checkout -b feature`. Plain `git branch feature` creates the branch without switching.

cards.prompt: How do you bring another branch into your current one?
cards.note: If your branch is simply behind, Git fast-forwards. Otherwise it creates a merge commit, and on conflicts you resolve the marked spots by hand.

cards.prompt: How do you upload your commits to the remote?
cards.note: If the push is rejected because others pushed first, get their work with `git pull` first. Keep your hands off `--force` on shared branches.

cards.prompt: How do you fetch changes from the remote and merge them in one step?
cards.note: `git pull` is `git fetch` plus `git merge`. With `git pull --rebase` the history stays linear.

cards.prompt: How do you put unfinished changes aside briefly without committing?
cards.note: `git stash pop` brings them back. Handy when you need to switch branches in a hurry.

cards.prompt: How do you undo an already pushed commit without rewriting history?
cards.note: `revert` creates a new commit that reverses the changes. That is safe on shared branches, unlike `reset`, which rewrites history.

cards.prompt: Which file tells Git which files to ignore?
cards.note: Build folders, `.env` files with secrets and `node_modules` belong in it. Git only ignores already tracked files once you remove them with `git rm --cached`.

cards.prompt: Which command tells you which directory you are in?
cards.note: It stands for "print working directory". `cd ~` takes you home at any time, `cd -` back to the previous directory.

cards.prompt: How do you list all files, including hidden ones, with details?
cards.note: `-l` shows permissions, owner, size and date; `-a` includes files starting with a dot. Add `-h` for readable sizes such as 4.0K.

cards.prompt: How do you create a folder including any missing parent folders?
cards.note: `mkdir -p project/src/tests` creates every missing level at once. If the folder already exists, it doesn't complain.

cards.prompt: Which command creates an empty file or updates its timestamp?
cards.note: `touch notes.txt` creates the file if it is missing. If it already exists, only its modification time changes.

cards.prompt: How do you copy a folder with everything in it?
cards.note: Without `-r`, `cp` refuses to copy folders. `cp -a` also keeps permissions and timestamps.

cards.prompt: Which command moves or renames a file?
cards.note: To the shell, renaming is just moving under a new name: `mv old.txt new.txt`. With `-i`, `mv` asks before overwriting anything.

cards.prompt: How do you delete a folder and its contents without being asked?
cards.note: There is no recycle bin and no confirmation. Check with `ls` first what you are deleting, and read the path twice.

cards.prompt: Which command searches for text inside files?
cards.note: `grep -rn "TODO" src/` searches recursively and shows line numbers. `-i` ignores case.

cards.prompt: Which command searches the directory tree for files by name?
cards.note: `find . -name "*.log"` finds every log file below the current folder. Add `-mtime -1` to only get files changed in the last 24 hours.

cards.prompt: How do you make a script executable?
cards.note: Then run it with `./script.sh`. The numeric form `chmod 755` means the owner may do everything, everyone else may read and execute.

cards.prompt: How do you follow new lines of a log file live?
cards.note: `tail -f /var/log/syslog` prints new lines as soon as they are written. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

cards.prompt: Which command shows running processes interactively with CPU load?
cards.note: `htop` is the friendlier version with colours and mouse support, but often has to be installed first. Press `q` to quit either.

cards.prompt: How do you end a process whose PID you know?
cards.note: `kill 1234` politely asks the process to terminate. Only if it doesn't respond does `kill -9 1234` force it.

cards.prompt: How do you pass the output of one command into another?
cards.note: `ps aux | grep python` filters the process list. `>`, by contrast, writes to a file and overwrites it, while `>>` appends.

cards.prompt: How do you open an encrypted shell on a server?
cards.note: `ssh user@server` opens an encrypted shell. Keys instead of a password, set up with `ssh-keygen` and `ssh-copy-id`, are safer and more convenient.

cards.prompt: How do you run a single command with administrator rights?
cards.note: It stands for "superuser do". It asks for your own password, not root's, and logs who ran what.
